concepts.title: The Group Axioms
concepts.contentHtml:
A group is a set with an operation that satisfies four rules:

1. Closure: combining two elements gives another element in the set
2. Associativity: (a • b) • c = a • (b • c)
3. Identity: there's an element e where a • e = e • a = a
4. Inverses: every element a has an a⁻¹ where a • a⁻¹ = e

Groups capture the essence of symmetry — the ways you can transform something and still have it look the same.
mathExpressions: (G, \cdot) \text{ with } e \in G, \; a^{-1} \in G \; \forall a

concepts.title: Examples of Groups
concepts.contentHtml:
(ℤ, +): Integers under addition. Identity = 0. Inverse of 5 is -5.

(ℤ/nℤ, +): Integers mod n. This is "clock arithmetic" — it's a group!

Symmetries of a square: 4 rotations + 4 reflections = 8 elements. This is the dihedral group D₄.

Non-example: Natural numbers under addition. No inverses (can't have -3 in ℕ), so not a group.

concepts.title: Abelian vs Non-Abelian
concepts.contentHtml:
A group is abelian (commutative) if a • b = b • a for all elements.

(ℤ, +) is abelian: 3 + 5 = 5 + 3. ✓

The symmetries of a square are non-abelian: rotating then reflecting is different from reflecting then rotating!

Non-commutativity is the source of much of group theory's richness and difficulty. It's also why matrix multiplication is non-commutative — matrices form a group (GLₙ).

title: Subgroups & Cyclic Groups
description: Groups within groups and the power of generators

concepts.title: Subgroups
concepts.contentHtml:
A subgroup H of G is a subset that is itself a group under the same operation.

The even integers are a subgroup of (ℤ, +). The rotations of a square are a subgroup of D₄.

Lagrange's Theorem: The size of a subgroup always divides the size of the group. If |G| = 12, subgroups can only have size 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, or 12.

This dramatically limits what subgroups can exist!

concepts.title: Cyclic Groups
concepts.contentHtml:
A cyclic group is generated by a single element — every element is a power of that generator.

ℤ/6ℤ is cyclic: generated by 1 (or by 5). Every element is a sum of 1's.

The rotations of an n-gon form a cyclic group of order n: one rotation generates all others.

Every group of prime order is cyclic. This is a direct consequence of Lagrange's theorem!

concepts.title: Cosets & Quotient Groups
concepts.contentHtml:
A coset of H in G is a "shifted copy" of H: gH = {gh : h ∈ H}.

Cosets partition the group into equal-sized pieces. The number of cosets is |G|/|H| — this is why Lagrange's theorem works.

If H is a normal subgroup (gHg⁻¹ = H for all g), the cosets themselves form a group called the quotient group G/H. This is how you "divide" groups.

concepts.title: The Symmetric Group Sₙ
concepts.contentHtml:
The symmetric group Sₙ is the group of all permutations (rearrangements) of n objects.

S₃ has 3! = 6 elements. S₄ has 4! = 24 elements. Sₙ has n! elements.

Cayley's Theorem: Every group is isomorphic to a subgroup of some Sₙ. This means permutation groups are universal — they contain every possible group structure!

concepts.title: Cycle Notation
concepts.contentHtml:
Cycle notation is a compact way to write permutations.

(1 3 2) means: 1→3, 3→2, 2→1. It's a 3-cycle.

Every permutation decomposes uniquely into disjoint cycles. (1 3)(2 4) means: swap 1↔3 and swap 2↔4 simultaneously.

Transpositions are 2-cycles like (1 2). Every permutation can be written as a product of transpositions.

concepts.title: Even & Odd Permutations
concepts.contentHtml:
A permutation is even if it's a product of an even number of transpositions, and odd otherwise.

The alternating group Aₙ consists of all even permutations. It has n!/2 elements and is always a normal subgroup of Sₙ.

A₅ is the smallest non-abelian simple group (no normal subgroups except {e} and itself). This is why there's no general formula for roots of polynomials of degree ≥ 5 (Abel-Ruffini theorem)!

concepts.title: Group Homomorphisms
concepts.contentHtml:
A homomorphism is a function between groups that preserves the operation: f(ab) = f(a)f(b).

Example: det: GLₙ → ℝ* sends matrices to their determinants. det(AB) = det(A)·det(B). ✓

The kernel of a homomorphism is the set mapped to the identity. It's always a normal subgroup. For det, the kernel is SLₙ (matrices with determinant 1).

The First Isomorphism Theorem: G/ker(f) ≅ im(f). Quotient out what's collapsed, and you get the image.

concepts.title: Symmetry in Physics
concepts.contentHtml:
Noether's Theorem: Every continuous symmetry of a physical system corresponds to a conserved quantity.

• Translational symmetry ↔ Conservation of momentum
• Rotational symmetry ↔ Conservation of angular momentum
• Time symmetry ↔ Conservation of energy

The Standard Model of particle physics is built on the symmetry group SU(3) × SU(2) × U(1). Different particles are representations of this group.

concepts.title: Groups in Chemistry, Music, and More
concepts.contentHtml:
Chemistry: Molecular symmetry groups predict which spectral transitions are allowed, which molecules are chiral, and how crystals form. The 230 crystallographic space groups classify all possible crystal structures.

Music theory: The twelve musical notes form ℤ/12ℤ. Transposition and inversion are group operations. Twelve-tone serialism is group theory applied to composition.

Rubik's Cube: The moves form a group with 43,252,003,274,489,856,000 elements. Group theory proved it can always be solved in ≤20 moves.
